abstract.p: Horizontal supply chain collaboration (HSCC) offers substantial cost savings and carbon footprint reductions, yet commercial adoption remains hindered by non-scalable gain-sharing mechanisms and operational disruption risks. This study presents a scalable two-stage hierarchical framework for post-Pareto selection, integrating a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear program (MILP, Level 1) with an Equal Profit Method linear program (EPML, Level 2) to optimize multi-objective routing and equitable profit allocation across multi-partner logistics networks. Evaluated on a medium-scale benchmark network (15 partners, 8 demand nodes, and 50 stochastic scenarios), the framework achieves an alliance-wide cost reduction of 18.42% and a carbon reduction of 14.10% relative to non-cooperative baselines. At Level 2, the EPML engine executes in 0.32 s for 15 partners and 1.87 s for 30 partners, overcoming the exponential computational bottlenecks of traditional cooperative game theory methods while theoretically guaranteeing expected individual rationality $\left(E\left[\pi_i\right] \geq \pi_i^0\right)$, where $E\left[\pi_i\right]$ denotes partner $i$'s expected collaborative profit and $\pi_i^0$ denotes that partner's standalone baseline profit—provided that the selected physical solution satisfies the net-synergy feasibility condition $(\sum_{i \in I} E\left[\pi_i\right] \geq \sum_{i \in I} \pi_i^0)$, where $I$ is the set of alliance partners. The framework also achieves empirically verified core stability, with $e_{\max} \leq 0$, where $e_{\max}$ denotes the maximum excess across the tested subcoalition. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates robust customer fulfillment (99.59% service level) under high shortfall penalties $\left(p_j^{\text {pen}} \geq 2.5 \times p_j^{\text {sell}}\right)$ and a marginal abatement cost (MAC) of \$2,318.68 per metric ton of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO$_2$e) at executive compromise configurations. To facilitate industry adoption, we translate these algorithmic outputs into a practical 4-step managerial decision protocol balancing ex-ante contractual rules, ex-post financial settlements, and alliance-level greenhouse gas (GHG) reporting boundaries. The framework effectively resolves the trade-off between allocation fairness and computational scalability in stochastic environments, providing supply chain decision-makers with a practical, mathematically rigorous, and computationally efficient post-Pareto decision-support tool to establish stable, equitable, and resilient horizontal logistics coalitions.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The design of horizontal supply chain collaboration (HSCC)—where firms at the same echelon pool logistics assets, transportation capacity, and distribution networks—has attracted growing attention under the convergence of Industry 5.0 sustainability mandates and structural supply chain volatility [1], [2]. This operational imperative is further accelerated by global regulatory frameworks, such as the European Union (EU) Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Standard [3]. Under these standards, Scope 3 emissions—specifically Category 1 (purchased goods and services) and Category 4 (upstream transportation and distribution)—represent 70–90% of a firm’s total carbon footprint, yet remain notoriously difficult to abate through unilateral actions [4]. While operational literature has quantified cost reductions of 15–30% through demand consolidation [5], 18–25% Scope 3 emission abatement via consolidated shipments [6], and enhanced structural resilience through cross-chain asset redundancy [7], integrating these three dimensions into a single, mathematically tractable optimization framework remains an open challenge. Existing contributions address subsets of these performance metrics—such as robust cost optimization [8], stochastic carbon–cost trade-offs [9], or cost–resilience balances [10]—as isolated problems; none unifies economic efficiency, Scope 3 environmental abatement, and disruption resilience simultaneously within a multi-objective stochastic design.

Despite documented theoretical gains, a persistent “Collaborative Paradox” hinders real-world implementation: While strategic logistics alliances promise substantial systemic benefits, empirical studies indicate that over half of horizontal logistics partnerships dissolve within two years. This high failure rate stems from two structural barriers:
• Asymmetric Gain Distribution: Participants fear opportunistic behavior and uncompensated asset exposure when cost reductions are not distributed in a demonstrably fair manner.

• Operational vs. Financial Misalignment: Post-hoc gain-sharing models fail to dynamically link financial redistribution with stochastic operational disruptions, leading to partner dissatisfaction when actual operational realities deviate from expected baseline plans.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related literature and highlights structural research gaps. Section 3 presents the mathematical nomenclature, formulates the Level 1 tri-objective stochastic MILP model, establishes the standalone non-cooperative baseline model, and details the Level 2 EPML gain-sharing model. Section 4 details the solution methodology, including the augmented epsilon-constraint method (AUGMECON2) Pareto solver, the hybrid genetic algorithm–linear programming (GA-LP) matheuristic, and the scenario generation and reduction engine via the Gaussian copula and k-means clustering. Section 5 provides computational validation, tri-objective trade-off analyses, and presents the numerical results of the comparative benchmarking of gain-sharing mechanisms against classical approaches. Section 6 proposes an in-depth discussion interpreting the results from strategic, operational, and environmental perspectives, while addressing limitations and future directions. Finally, Section 7 summarizes findings and discusses managerial implications.

sec.title: 2. Literature review
sec.p: The pursuit of horizontally coordinated supply chains has intensified as firms seek simultaneous improvements in cost efficiency, environmental accountability, and structural robustness against disruptions. This literature review systematically examines four interconnected streams that collectively motivate the proposed two-stage hierarchical framework: (i) HSCC and tri-objective synergies, (ii) stochastic optimization and multi-objective solution methodologies, (iii) cost and profit allocation mechanisms, and (iv) hierarchical versus integrated optimization architectures. Across these streams, we identify persistent gaps that the present work seeks to address.

sec.title: 2.1. Horizontal supply chain collaboration and tri-objective synergies
sec.p: HSCC involves cooperative arrangements among firms operating at the same echelon, enabling joint logistics, asset sharing, and capacity consolidation that generate mutual efficiencies unattainable through unilateral optimization [11], [12]. Recent scholarship has documented substantial cost savings and service-level improvements arising from collaborative transportation planning, pooled warehousing, and shared fulfillment networks [13], [14]. Çerçi et al. [15] provide a contemporary taxonomy of horizontal logistics partnerships, emphasizing that digital platform enablers have expanded collaboration from bilateral carrier alliances to multi-party ecosystems with real-time matching capabilities. Parallel work by Mrabti et al. [3] synthesizes evidence that HSCC constitutes one of the most effective levers for addressing sustainability challenges in freight networks, particularly through load factor optimization and vehicle-kilometer reduction.

Despite these advances, integrating environmental and resilience objectives alongside economic cost minimization within HSCC models has traditionally been addressed primarily through pairwise extensions rather than fully unified frameworks. The Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol identifies Scope 3 emissions—particularly Categories 1 (purchased goods and services) and 4 (upstream transportation and distribution)—as representing 70–90% of total corporate carbon footprints [4]. While early HSCC formulations treated emissions as secondary constraints or evaluated disruption resilience through post-hoc sensitivity analyses [16], recent scholarship has advanced bi-objective paradigms. Specifically, cost–carbon trade-offs have been examined in collaborative logistics settings [17], [18], and green or resilient supply chain network designs under uncertainty have been formulated separately [6], [8], [9], [10]. However, existing frameworks typically isolate environmental abatement from structural disruption risks. The simultaneous integration of expected logistics costs, Scope 3 emissions quantified via consolidated route emission factors (

sec.title: 2.2. Stochastic optimization and multi-objective frameworks in supply chains
sec.p: Two-stage stochastic programming (SP) has established itself as a foundational paradigm for supply chain network design under uncertainty, wherein strategic first-stage decisions (facility activation) precede operational recourse actions (flow allocation and shortfall management) conditioned on realized scenarios [19], [20]. Scenario generation and reduction techniques are similarly well-established: Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) ensures uniform coverage across continuous parameter distributions, while copula-based approaches capture complex spatial dependence structures among correlated market demands and disruption severities [21]. Subsequent scenario reduction via $k$-means clustering or backward reduction algorithms preserves distributional fidelity while maintaining computational tractability [22]. Recent contributions demonstrate the effectiveness of two-stage stochastic frameworks across closed-loop and perishable logistics systems under multi-dimensional uncertainty [23], [24].

When multiple conflicting objectives are introduced, AUGMECON2 serves as a standard exact approach for generating non-dominated Pareto frontiers in multi-objective integer programming [25], guaranteeing Pareto optimality through slack variable augmentation and overcoming the limitations of weighted-sum methods on non-convex regions [26]. For large-scale NP-hard instances, hybrid matheuristics combining evolutionary search with exact mathematical programming sub-solvers offer a practical trade-off between solution quality and computational efficiency [27]. While AUGMECON2 and matheuristics are well-documented in multi-objective optimization, exact AUGMECON2 resolution encounters severe computational bottlenecks when scaled to tri-objective stochastic MILPs with dense recourse scenario trees. This computational boundary motivates pairing exact Pareto mapping with a scalable hybrid GA-LP matheuristic for large-scale instances.

sec.title: 2.3. Cost/profit allocation and gain-sharing mechanisms
sec.p:
The allocation of collaborative cost savings among coalition members has traditionally been addressed through cooperative game-theoretic solution concepts. The Shapley value distributes gains according to marginal contributions across all coalition permutations [28], while the nucleolus minimizes the maximum dissatisfaction of any sub-coalition [29], and the core ensures that no subset of players has an incentive to deviate [29]. These axiomatic methods possess strong normative appeal; however, their application to large-scale supply chain networks is severely limited by an exponential computational complexity of

sec.p:
Bilevel and hierarchical optimization architectures have attracted growing interest in collaborative network design, where strategic decisions at an upper level constrain operational decisions at a lower level [33], [34]. In the context of HSCC, a critical architectural question arises: should physical flow decisions and financial allocation decisions be optimized jointly within a single integrated model, or decomposed into a hierarchical sequence? Crucially, Level 2 functions as a post-Pareto selection layer: after Level 1 constructs the non-dominated Pareto frontier across physical operational objectives (cost, emissions, disruption risk), Level 2 evaluates the financial viability and equity of candidate physical Pareto solutions. Decision-makers can thus verify whether a selected physical compromise point (e.g., Point C) yields an equitable and individually rational financial distribution across all participants. By decoupling physical optimization from financial allocation, this sequential architecture mathematically eliminates non-convex MINLP bottlenecks, maintains a linear MILP formulation at Level 1 and a convex LP at Level 2, and guarantees that Level 2 executes in 0.32 s for 15 partners and 1.87 s for 30 partners. In multi-echelon networks, market power asymmetries often prevent small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) from joining collaborative freight consortia [64], [65]. sec.title: 6.3. Dynamic gain-sharing and automated re-negotiation
sec.p:
In volatile operational environments, physical disruption events—such as port congestion, vehicle breakdowns, or severe weather—alter optimal routing paths and immediately render fixed, ex-ante cost-allocation contracts obsolete [60], [66]. Traditional cooperative game-theoretic solvers are incapable of real-time execution in large networks (

This computational speed transforms gain-sharing from a static, post-hoc accounting exercise into a dynamic operational decision tool [62], [67]. Logistics managers can re-run the EPML allocation algorithm rapidly whenever operational disruptions or demand shifts occur, supporting timely and transparent contractual gain-sharing updates across coalition partners [67].

Decoupling Environmental Mandates from Financial Disputes: The proposed two-stage hierarchical architecture decouples physical multi-objective trade-offs (Cost vs. Scope 3 emissions vs. Resilience) from inter-firm financial negotiations. This separation simplifies collaborative governance, accelerates executive consensus, while providing a quantitative basis for transparent monitoring and reporting of supply-chain emissions. sec.title: 6.4. Operational scope and network structure boundaries
sec.p: While the proposed framework demonstrates robust computational performance and high allocation equity, the operational interpretation of these findings must be contextualized within the structural boundaries of the model. The formulation assumes a single-period, single-echelon, direct-shipping logistics network. These assumptions are intentionally chosen to isolate the structural mechanics of the endogenous LP-based gain-sharing engine and the tri-objective Pareto trade-offs without confounding variables. Consequently, specific numerical findings—such as sub-second allocation solve times (1.87 s for 30 partners) and flow rerouting percentages—reflect this single-tier direct distribution context and should not be automatically extrapolated to multi-echelon networks featuring intermediate consolidation hubs, multi-tier inventory holding, or complex lead-time dynamics without appropriate architectural adaptations.
